pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Solve addition and subtraction WORD PROBLEMS within 10 using objects or drawings — applying the combining/taking-away concepts to real situations by modelling them concretely.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'solve one-step problems that involve addition and subtraction, using concrete objects and pictorial representations, and missing number problems'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.2 'solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10… by using objects or drawings'; the CGI problem taxonomy (add-to, take-from, put-together/take-apart, compare — with the unknown in various positions) frames difficulty.
• Operational details — The core skill is MODELLING: read/hear the situation, represent it with objects or a drawing, then read the answer off the model. Vary the problem STRUCTURE (result-unknown is easiest; change-unknown and start-unknown are harder) and the unknown POSITION, not just the numbers. Discourage keyword-matching ('altogether = add'); instead have children act out or draw what is happening. Keep totals within 10 so the count is manageable.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): solve a result-unknown add-to or take-from story with counters. Tier B (age 5): choose objects/drawing to model a put-together or take-apart problem and state the answer. Tier C (age 5-6): model a change-unknown or simple compare problem and explain how the drawing matches the story.
bestPractices: Teach modelling, not keyword-spotting: children act out or draw the SITUATION and read the answer from it, so 'altogether'/'left' don't become false triggers for +/−.
Systematically vary problem structure and unknown position (result-, change-, start-unknown; compare) so children build a robust sense of the operations, not one rote pattern.
Use consistent representations (counters, part-whole, bar/tape) so the model itself carries meaning across problems.
Have children retell the problem in their own words and point to each quantity in their model, tying language to representation to answer.
Start with result-unknown, keep numbers within 10, and introduce missing-number/compare forms only once modelling of simple problems is secure.
keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes acted on to match the story
Children's drawings/jottings (dots, crossing-out) of the situation
Part-part-whole model mapping story quantities to parts and whole
Simple bar/tape model for compare problems ('how many more')
Five-frame/ten-frame to organise the objects being combined or removed
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching ('altogether'→add, 'left'→subtract) instead of modelling the situation, which fails on compare and change/start-unknown problems.
Modelling only result-unknown structures and being stuck when the unknown is the change or the start.
Grabbing the two numbers in the problem and combining them regardless of what the story describes.
Miscounting the objects when acting out, or not matching the drawing to the actual quantities in the story.
For compare problems, adding the two amounts instead of finding the difference.

learn.summary: Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1): solve one-step addition and subtraction word problems within 10 by MODELLING the situation with objects or drawings, then reading the answer off the model. The core skill is representing what the story describes (things arriving, leaving, two groups combined, two groups compared, or a mystery start), not keyword-matching. Systematically vary problem structure and unknown position; keep totals within 10 so counting stays manageable.

activities.title: Story-modelling with counters and a mat
feedback: Check that the model matches the STORY, not just that the number is right: ask 'show me with the counters what happens to the apples.'
If the child combines both numbers (answers 8 for the apples, i.e. 6+2), have them act the take-away story out step by step with counters before counting, tying it to the removing action.
For the joining story, ask 'did the number get bigger or smaller — why?' to connect the action to the operation.
If the set-up is correct but the count slips, scaffold one-to-one counting; the modelling is sound, so do not reteach it.
activities.rationale: At this age, word-problem solving IS modelling: reading/hearing the situation, representing it concretely, and reading the result off the representation. Acting out the situation avoids the keyword-matching that fails on harder structures.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems, including missing-number problems, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
K.OA.2: solve addition and subtraction word problems within 10 using objects or drawings.
Problem difficulty is governed by situation structure and unknown position (Cognitively Guided Instruction taxonomy); teaching modelling rather than keyword-matching improves problem solving.
learnerActions: Listen to or look at a short situation, e.g. 'There are 6 apples on the tree; the wind blows 2 down.'
Take 6 apple counters and place them on a mat to match the start of the story.
Act out what happens — move the 2 fallen apples to the ground, or cross them out on a drawing.
Count what is left on the tree and say the answer aloud (4).
Retell the story in your own words and point to each quantity (the 6, the 2, what's left) in your model.
Repeat with a joining story, e.g. 'Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now?', adding counters to match and reading off the total (7).
activities.intendedInsight: You don't need a rule to decide 'add' or 'subtract' — you build what actually happened in the story with objects, and the answer is simply what you can then see and count.

activities.title: Part-whole and compare: beyond result-unknown
feedback: If the child adds the two numbers for the part-unknown (4 + 7 = 11), build the whole (7) and the known part (4) with counters so the gap becomes visible; use a part-whole or bar layout.
For compare problems, if the child adds the two amounts, line the groups up and point to the extra ones to show the difference is what's being asked.
Ask 'how many altogether, and how many do you already know?' to surface which quantity is missing.
Praise a correct layout even before the count, then support careful counting if needed.
activities.rationale: Difficulty is strongly influenced by situation structure and unknown position (as well as number size); missing-part, change-unknown, start-unknown and compare problems defeat keyword rules and rote result-unknown patterns, so they are introduced and modelled explicitly once simple problems are secure.
sourceClaims: Problem difficulty is governed by situation structure and unknown position (Cognitively Guided Instruction taxonomy); teaching modelling rather than keyword-matching improves problem solving.
Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems, including missing-number problems, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Model a put-together problem with a missing part, e.g. 'There are 4 red counters and some blue ones, 7 altogether — how many are blue?'
Build the whole (7) and lay out the known part (4) using a part-part-whole frame.
Find the gap — the blue counters needed to fill the whole — and count them to give the answer (3).
Model a simple compare problem, e.g. 'how many more', by lining up two groups side by side (a bar/tape layout) and finding the difference.
For each problem, say whether it is a putting-together story or a comparing story, and explain how your drawing matches the words.
activities.intendedInsight: When the unknown is a part or a difference, you still build the situation — lay out what you know and find what's missing — rather than just combining the two numbers you can see.

activities.title: Narrate and show (talk alongside the model)
feedback: Prompt the child to connect language to representation: 'show me the part where things leave.'
If narration drifts from the model, pause and re-anchor each spoken quantity to a group of objects.

Keep the talk tied to acting on objects: the age-appropriate expectation is work with concrete objects and pictorial representations, so narration is intended to accompany modelling rather than replace it.
activities.rationale: Retelling the problem and pointing to each quantity ties language to representation to answer. Dialogue can develop sense-making; because the curriculum for this age expects work with concrete objects and drawings, talk is intended to accompany acting on objects, and its standalone efficacy is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Tell an adult or peer what is happening in the story in your own words.
As you narrate, show each step on the objects or drawing ('first there were six… then two fell…').
Answer prompts such as 'which part do you already know?' and 'what are we trying to find?' while pointing to the model.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the story into your own words and linking each phrase to a quantity in your model builds sense-making, so the words guide the action rather than triggering a reflex operation.

constraints: Teach modelling, not keyword-spotting: 'altogether'/'left'/'more' must not become fixed triggers for + or −, because they fail on compare, change-unknown and start-unknown problems.
Keep totals within 10 so counting is manageable; start with result-unknown and introduce missing-number and compare forms only once simple modelling is secure.
Systematically vary problem structure (add-to, take-from, put-together/take-apart, compare) and unknown position (result-, change-, start-unknown), not just the numbers.

A fixed single-story illustration (tap to count, reveal the answer) can anchor one problem's modelling but cannot let the child model varied structures or make their own drawing; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole skill.

Picture-based multiple-choice items can check whether a child recognises/applies the right operation, but a scored recognition format does not itself elicit the child building a model and can be answered by keyword-matching; if used, pair each item with a picture and avoid phrasing answerable by keyword alone.
Use consistent representations (counters/cubes, part-part-whole, bar/tape, five-/ten-frame) so the model itself carries meaning across problems.

Interactive affordances are optional illustrations, not requirements: e.g. dragging objects onto a mat, crossing out, a part-whole/bar frame to organise quantities, narrated scenes, auto-varying the problem type. These make the mechanism concrete but need not all be present.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a scored recognition format 'can't develop the modelling process' and that talk alone is a 'weak' route; these are plausible but not established as universal laws by the cited sources. They have been narrowed to observable affordances / curriculum-grounded qualifications with 'may'/'intended' framing.

The legacy row rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing ('no spatial dimension to exploit'); this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped rather than asserted. Physical manipulatives (counters/cubes) remain central and are themselves tactile.

Self-audit of the diagnostic arithmetic: (1) 6 apples, 2 eaten → 4 left; (2) 3 marbles + 4 → 7; (3) 4 red, 7 total → 3 blue. All correct. The error trace 'answers 8 for the apples' corresponds to 6+2 (combining regardless of story) and 'answers 11' corresponds to 4+7 (adding instead of finding the missing part) — both coherent misconception traces, retained as feedback cues.
Internal prerequisite/reteach reference codes from the original row were not migrated into learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: Show me with the counters what happens to the apples.
For the marbles, did the number get bigger or smaller — why?
How many counters altogether in the last one, and how many do you already know?
Which of these was a taking-away story and which was a putting-together story?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) 4; (2) 7; (3) 3 — with the situation modelled on the counters (take-away, join, and part-unknown respectively).

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines both numbers whatever the story — adds 6 and 2 for the take-away problem, or applies one default operation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act the story out with counters step by step before counting; link it to the take-away representation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 8 for the apples problem.

errorPatterns.pattern: Part-unknown problem solved by adding the two numbers (4 red, 7 total → 4 + 7 = 11) rather than finding the missing part.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the whole (7) and the known part (4) with counters and see the gap; use a part-whole / bar layout.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 11 for the blue counters.

errorPatterns.pattern: Right representation but miscounts the objects.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold one-to-one counting; the modelling is sound, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct set-up (removes / joins / finds the gap) but the count slips.

responseLevels.gap: Applies one default operation regardless of the story; cannot model the situation.
responseLevels.full: Models each situation with objects and solves take-away, join, and part-unknown problems within 10 correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown add and take-away by modelling, but the part-unknown problem defaults to adding the two numbers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Use the counters to solve these. (1) There are 6 apples and 2 are eaten — how many are left? (2) Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now? (3) There are 4 red counters and some blue ones, 7 altogether — how many are blue?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The result-unknown take-away and join (1, 2) are straightforward; the put-together-with-part-unknown (3) is harder and reveals whether the child models the situation or just operates on the two visible numbers. Watch whether they act the story out with counters (as the topic requires) or grab the numbers and apply a default operation.
